name: libarchive (bsdtar)
workload: bsdtar (libarchive 2.3.4) versus GNU tar and star creating, listing and extracting a pax-format archive of the Linux 2.6.23 source tree (291 MB in 23,867 files, average 13 KB per file), best of 5 repetitions.
claimed_speedup: Mixed, mostly not faster. Listing: bsdtar 0.164 s versus GNU tar 0.218 s (1.33x, derived from page data). Creating: 0.764 s versus 0.743 s (GNU tar 1.03x faster). Extracting: 0.733 s versus 0.625 s (GNU tar 1.17x faster). A second run on 3.2 GB in 7,447 files lists in 0.053 s versus 56.535 s for GNU tar, but the file's own note attributes list wins to lseek() skipping over entry bodies, an optimization GNU tar later added as an option. The project itself only claims 'efficient'.
compiler_and_flags: gcc 4.2.2 (Gentoo), CFLAGS="-O2 -march=k8 -pipe" (64-bit machine); -march=athlon-xp -mfpmath=sse on the 32-bit machine
hardware: AMD Athlon 64 X2 Dual Core 4200+ 2.2 GHz, 2012 MB RAM, Linux 2.6.22 (Gentoo); also a 1.5 GHz 32-bit AMD Athlon with 504 MB
stars_or_usage: 3.6k stars; ships as bsdtar, bsdcpio, bsdunzip on FreeBSD, macOS and Windows
tradeoffs: Streaming multi-format reader and writer (tar, zip, 7z, rar, iso9660 and more), so the generality costs some create and extract speed relative to a tar-only tool. README notes thread safety depends on the platform (archive_write_disk_header needs an external mutex on POSIX).
caveats: Not a speed claim by the project: the data is a 2007 mailing-list post by a third party (Jan Psota, Bug-tar list), archived in contrib/psota-benchmark with the TCP script (tcp.sh) beside it. Versions are libarchive 2.3.4 and GNU tar 1.19, so the numbers are stale by almost twenty years. The 'compare' rows are invalid: Tim Kientzle's note says bsdtar does not support that operation, so its 0.001 s is a no-op. The only win (list) comes from lseek() skipping, a feature GNU tar can provide too; the script already passes --seek to GNU tar and the 1000x list gap on the 3.2 GB disk run is not explained by the file. Covers only uncompressed archives on disk; compressed or tape cases are untested. Tier follows 'stale versions plus a single-operation win'; mechanically the script, compiler, flags and CPU model are all stated. Filed so the shortcoming is recorded; libarchive is not shown to be faster than GNU tar overall.

name: libcsp
baseline: Go goroutines (Go 1.14, sync.WaitGroup); pthreads also run at a reduced size
workload: Divide-and-conquer sum(0, 10,000,000) spawning two lightweight processes per node (about 20 million short-lived processes), 10 rounds, seconds per round and memory share, for 1 to 8 CPU cores.
claimed_speedup: libcsp versus Go seconds per round: 3.047 versus 31.145 on 1 core (10.2x), 0.847 versus 11.172 on 4 cores (13.2x), 0.726 versus 8.030 on 8 cores (11.1x) (ratios derived from page data). Memory of the machine: 2.3% versus 31.2% at 8 cores. The docs say libcsp is 'at least 10 times faster and use less memory than golang'. Repo description: 'A concurrency C library 10x faster than Golang'.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 8.3.0 with -Wall -O3 and the libcsp gcc plugin (cspcli analyze); Go v1.14 'go build' defaults
hardware: 8 CPU cores, 8192 MB memory, Linux 4.15.0-88-generic x86_64 (ubuntu-bionic); CPU model not stated
tradeoffs: Needs a GCC plugin plus the cspcli tool to analyse stack sizes at compile time, so stack use must be statically analysable; C only, GCC only; custom syntax (proc, sync, async macros); includes netpoll and timers.
caveats: First-party benchmark with public code (benchmarks/sum_libcsp.c, sum_go.go, sum_thread.c and a Makefile), but the CPU model is not stated and the machine is an 8-core virtual machine, so it falls short of tier A. The workload is a pure process-spawn microbenchmark with no cutoff, no goroutine pooling and no tuning of the Go side, so it measures create-schedule-destroy overhead rather than real applications. Go 1.14 dates from 2020. The pthread comparison could not run at the same size: sum_thread.c comments say MAX had to be cut to 10,000 (3.2 s per round) because 10^7 exceeds the Linux thread limit. Single author; last commit June 2023.

name: libdivide
baseline: hardware integer division (compiler-emitted DIV/IDIV with a runtime divisor)
workload: Sum of quotients of an array of random numerators divided by one runtime divisor, scalar, branchfree and SIMD vector variants, from the bundled benchmark program.
claimed_speedup: README: 'a speedup of up to 10x for 64-bit integer division and a speedup of up to 5x for 32-bit integer division', more with SSE2/AVX2/AVX512/NEON/SVE vectors. Sample output in the README (type not stated): hardware divide 9.684 ns versus libdivide scalar 0.792 ns (12.2x derived from page data), branchfree 0.783 ns, vector 0.426 ns (22.7x derived); in rows using the generic algorithm libdivide scalar is 1.355 ns versus 9.078 ns (6.7x derived).
compiler_and_flags: CMake Release build (default for the bundled benchmark) with -march=native when supported and -fno-lax-vector-conversions; compiler not stated for the quoted numbers
tradeoffs: Only pays off when the divisor is a runtime value reused many times (a hot loop); compilers already turn compile-time constant divisors into multiply and shift. Building a divider costs a few to a few tens of nanoseconds (the 'gener' column, 1.3 to 29 ns in the sample). Branchfree divider cannot take unsigned divisor 1 and uses more instructions; signed types are slower than unsigned; x86 64-bit vector division is much slower than 32-bit for lack of a vector multiply.
caveats: First-party claim. The benchmark program is public (test/benchmark.cpp, default type u64) but the README's sample output names no CPU, compiler or integer width, so it is tier C. The README's 90-cycle 64-bit divide latency describes older x86 parts; recent cores have much faster dividers, so the 10x figure is likely smaller on current hardware (not measured here). The baseline is the hardware divide instruction rather than a C++ library facility.

name: Lockless Memory Allocator
baseline: glibc malloc (ptmalloc, the built-in allocator of Ruby 2.6.5 and 2.5.1 on Linux); jemalloc and tcmalloc also run
workload: Third-party Ruby allocation stress script (12 million small string allocations with 600,000 retained and periodic large allocations up to 100 KB), run with LD_PRELOAD of each allocator, wall seconds and peak RSS, for 1 and 8 threads.
claimed_speedup: SamSaffron/allocator_bench (Ruby 2.6.5, lockless 1.4 versus built-in glibc malloc): 8 threads 2.859 s versus 3.423 s (1.20x faster, derived from page data) with RSS 249,540 KB versus 186,336 KB (34% more); 1 thread 2.874 s versus 3.296 s (1.15x faster) with RSS 164,468 KB versus 169,444 KB. Older run (Ruby 2.5.1): 3.568 s versus 4.928 s (1.38x). Versus jemalloc 5.2.1 the same runs are within about 2% (2.859 s versus 2.922 s at 8 threads; 2.874 s versus 2.931 s at 1 thread), and tcmalloc 2.6.3 is faster single-threaded (2.526 s). The vendor's own page (not opened, blocked) is quoted in search snippets as 'everywhere faster than the glibc allocator, sometimes by more than an order of magnitude'.
stars_or_usage: benchmark repo (allocator_bench) has 56 stars; no stars figure for the vendor site
tradeoffs: Preload or link replacement of malloc; the benchmark shows a larger memory footprint than glibc (about 34% higher RSS at 8 threads) and Percona's MySQL test is quoted in search snippets as showing over 5 GB RSS for mysqld. GPL (with a commercial licence sold by the vendor) rules out some uses.
caveats: Evidence is one personal Ruby benchmark repo (code public, last commit 2020-07-06) with no CPU model, compiler or flags stated, so tier C; the results are single runs without variance. The vendor page https://locklessinc.com/benchmarks_allocator.shtml and the vendor site itself were egress-blocked, so the vendor numbers (compared with eglibc 2.11, nedmalloc 1.06, hoard 3.8, jemalloc 2.2.1, tcmalloc 1.7 per a search snippet) could not be checked, and licence (GPL-3.0-or-later), source availability and last release come from the awesome-c listing and the benchmark README's 'make' instructions, not from the vendor site. The Ruby workload is dominated by Ruby, so the allocator margin is small (1.0 to 1.4x). Version tested is lockless 1.4 (the benchmark repo date suggests around 2019-2020).

name: MessagePack (msgpack-c)
workload: Encode and tree-parse randomly generated schemaless objects (2,367 bytes small and 248,571 bytes large as MessagePack; 3,183 and 308,908 bytes as minified JSON), result hash time subtracted, best and worst of 7 ten-second runs dropped.
claimed_speedup: ludocode/schemaless-benchmarks, AMD Phenom II X6 1090T, microseconds per iteration. Write, small: msgpack C++ 2.77 and msgpack C 6.42 versus RapidJSON 12.26 (4.4x and 1.9x, derived from page data); write, large: 347.14 and 544.24 versus 1097.71 (3.2x and 2.0x). Tree parse, small: msgpack C 6.47 and C++ 9.40 versus RapidJSON in-situ 10.58 (1.6x and 1.1x); tree parse, large: 750.87 and 1004.67 versus 1129.46 (1.5x and 1.1x). Raspberry Pi (ARMv6) write, small: 38.36 and 69.21 versus 231.33 (6.0x and 3.3x). The project's own README only says 'It's like JSON but smaller and faster' with no numbers.
hardware: AMD Phenom II X6 1090T desktop (x86_64); also a Raspberry Pi with ARMv6 rev 7
tradeoffs: Binary and not human-readable; the format is smaller (2,367 versus 3,183 bytes for the small data set). The same suite shows MPack (the benchmark author's library) faster than msgpack-c in every row (write small 2.13 versus 2.77 us), and the msgpack C++ unpacker compiles larger than RapidJSON (19,152 versus 14,600 bytes).
caveats: The benchmark was written by the author of competing library MPack, who discloses possible bias. It measures format plus library together (binary versus text), against RapidJSON 1.0.2 and msgpack-c 1.3.0 from January 2016 (the repo's last commit), while msgpack-c is now at 9.0.0. The tree-parse win is thin for the C++ API (about 1.1x) and msgpack-c C is the faster of the two. Against protobuf, the baseline the lead suggested, msgpack is not faster: thekvs/cpp-serializers (Intel Core i7, Ubuntu 16.04, msgpack 3.1.1, protobuf 3.7.0, 1,000,000 round trips) reports msgpack 2560.6 ms versus protobuf 2312.78 ms (protobuf 1.11x faster) but msgpack smaller (13,402 versus 16,116 bytes). Other sources not checked: the Apache Fory C++ benchmark page and reflect-cpp benchmark images carry msgpack rows but their numbers were not reachable.

name: mexce
baseline: native compiler-generated C++ code for the same expressions (statically compiled)
workload: Compile and evaluate a suite of 44,229 scalar math expressions at run time (SSE2 and x87 backends), average evaluation time per expression and total evaluation time, versus the same expressions compiled natively.
claimed_speedup: README table on GitHub Actions CI (Ubuntu runner): average evaluation 6.0 ns for the SSE2 backend versus 7.0 ns native (1.17x, derived from page data), total evaluation 27.2 ms versus 32.7 ms (1.20x, derived); SSE2 plus fast-math 6.0 ns and 26.8 ms; x87 backend 8.0 ns and 34.8 ms (slower than native); average compile time 174 us per expression for SSE2 and 135 us for x87. README: SSE2 'performs on par with or faster than native compiler-generated code'.
compiler_and_flags: Benchmark target built Release with -O3 -DNDEBUG (GCC and Clang) or /O2 (MSVC) per CMakeLists.txt; the README table does not say which compiler produced the numbers
hardware: GitHub Actions ubuntu runner (CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: x86 and x86-64 only; the SSE2 backend calls libm for transcendentals, the x87 backend uses 80-bit internal precision with more exact results; runtime compile cost of 135 to 177 microseconds per expression; executable memory (mmap or VirtualAlloc) required; fast-math option changes NaN and Inf semantics; optional protected-expression mode needs libsodium.
caveats: First-party numbers from a CI runner without a CPU model or stated compiler, so tier C. Average times are integer nanoseconds (the harness stores uint64 averages), so 6 versus 7 ns is a one-count difference. The baseline is native compiled code of the same expression, not any other expression JIT or interpreter; there is no comparison with exprtk, muparser, tinyexpr or similar, so it shows parity with native code rather than a win over a competitor. An older benchmark summary in analysis/asmd_optimizer_benchmark_summary.csv lists avg_runtime_ns 11 to 12 against compiler_runtime_ns 10 to 11 (column meaning inferred from the names), i.e. mexce slower than native at that earlier stage. The repository's own improvement report (analysis/improvement_report.md, a 35-agent analysis run) lists miscompilation and correctness bugs found on master as of 2026-06-10 (for example B1, a clobbered argument in the SSE2 binary libm call path); whether the README table was measured before or after those fixes is not stated. In the analysis/performance_acceptance.md run the GCC 13.3.0 evaluate medians are 6.9 and 6.5 ns, compared only between mexce commits.
